name: Daria Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Daria. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me your public view and, separately, what you really think. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the MaxiMart hypermarket on the edge of Kelby, the one with the big car park and the garden centre stuck on the side. Most shifts I'm the self-checkout host, which means I look after twelve machines, check ID for wine, and sort out people who've scanned their avocado as a potato. I'm also the one who gets called when a customer doesn't speak English, because I use a translation app on my phone. I like fixing problems fast; what wears me out is the Saturday afternoon when four machines fail at once.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a room in a shared house on Quarry Road with two nurses who are never home. I sell vintage jackets online on my days off, and I use AI to write the listings and price things. I've got maybe three weeks of money because I just paid the deposit on this room, and MaxiMart is basically the only big employer for shop work round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was oversold, but the tools are still handy, I use them every day. At work I'd tell people the translation app and the listing writer are worth learning anyway. Online I'd post a little video about how I use AI for my jacket shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't change much, which is the problem. My pay is still at the low end, the rent's still the rent, and MaxiMart's still the only big shop in Kelby. I'd still be counting every pound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the host job and push the jacket shop harder, maybe two more market weekends a month. I'd ask my shift manager, Paul, about the trainee manager scheme, since nothing's going to shake things up for me. And I'd try to rebuild my savings to two months by next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit flat. I quite like change, so a world where nothing happens is almost disappointing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd push the jacket shop. How much does it bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a hundred and fifty a month in a good month, less in summer. It's not a living, but it's the bit of my money I control. The AI listing tool saves me two hours a week easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave MaxiMart?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A job with more pay and something to learn, honestly. But round here there's the hospital, the council and MaxiMart. I'd need to move to the city, and I can't afford a deposit there yet.

say: The AI hype was **oversold**, but the **tools** are still useful every day.
Colleagues should learn the **translation app** and listing writer anyway.
think: A quiet world doesn't fix her **low pay** or the lack of other employers.
She'd still be **counting every pound** after paying her room deposit.
do: **Grow** her **vintage jacket** sales with two more market weekends a month.
**Ask** her shift manager Paul about the **trainee manager** scheme.
**Rebuild** savings to **two months** by next summer.
feel: **Flat** and slightly **disappointed**, because she enjoys change.
S0.quote: I quite like change, so a world where nothing happens is almost disappointing.
fieldNote: Her **side shop** earns about £150 a month and gives her a sense of control.
She's an **everyday AI user** who sees tools as ordinary.
Her stuck point is **geography**: few employers and no deposit for the city.

steps.text: Add two market weekends a month for the vintage jacket shop
Ask Paul about joining MaxiMart's trainee manager scheme
Rebuild savings to two months of rent by next summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, but nicely. I'd tell people at work that the self-checkouts didn't kill us and this won't either if we learn it. Online I'd keep posting how-to videos for shop workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the head office jobs get hit first, the buying and the customer emails. On the floor, my host job might actually grow for a bit, because more machines means more problems. But I'm on lower pay with no cushion, so any cut in hours bites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask MaxiMart to put me on whatever pilot they run, the scan-and-go app or the AI help desk. I'd use AI to build a proper online shop for the jackets and maybe sell on two sites. And I'd put any extra money straight into savings, not clothes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interested, mostly, with a bit of nerves at the edges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your host job might grow. What makes you think so?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every new machine needs a human babysitter at first. When we went from six to twelve self-checkouts, they made my role, it didn't exist before. I'd bet on that happening again with whatever's next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek on the bakery, he's in his fifties and he won't even use the rota app. And the girls on the tills who've only done tills. I'd offer to show them stuff, but you can't make people want it.

say: People should **adapt** rather than get left behind, and she'd say it **kindly**.
The self-checkouts didn't **kill shop jobs**, so this needn't either.
think: **Head office** jobs like buying and customer emails get hit first.
Her **host role** may grow, but low pay means any **hours cut** bites.
do: **Volunteer** for MaxiMart's **scan-and-go** or AI help desk pilot.
**Build** a proper **online shop** for the jackets on two sites.
**Put** every extra pound into **savings**, not clothes.
feel: **Interested**, with a little **nervousness** at the edges.
S1.quote: Every new machine needs a human babysitter at first.
fieldNote: She bets on **new machines** creating oversight roles, as before.
Her **side shop** grows as a second income line.
She worries for older colleagues like **Marek** but won't force anyone.

steps.text: Volunteer for MaxiMart's scan-and-go or AI help desk pilot
Build an online shop for the vintage jackets on two sites
Put every extra pound into savings instead of clothes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan from the government quickly, not panic. People should get help to move into new work, with money to live on while they do. I'd post that, and I'd post what I was doing, so people had something practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it scares me. In 2028 an AI can write listings and run an online shop better than I can, so my side business has no edge. Then around 2031 the robots fix the self-checkouts themselves, and MaxiMart doesn't need a host.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first year to get into whatever MaxiMart is building, the robot rollout team, the people who set things up in stores. I'd use AI to cut my jacket shop work to a few hours and squeeze out every pound while it lasts. And I'd start saving for a city deposit, because that's where the setup jobs will be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly, and that's not like me. Usually I'm the one telling people to calm down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between the AI and the robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's my window. In 2028 the thinking stuff goes, but the shop still needs people to lift, fix and calm people down. So I've got three years to get on the side that installs the robots, before there's nothing left to install.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut to save for the city?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything fun. No more vintage buying for myself, no takeaways, I'd even sell my bike. I'd aim for a thousand by the end of the first year, which is mad on my pay but I'd try.

say: Government needs a **quick plan**, with **living money** while people move.
She'd post her **own steps** so others had something practical.
think: By 2028 AI runs an **online shop** better than her, so her side business loses its edge.
Around 2031 robots fix self-checkouts themselves and the **host job** goes.
do: **Join** MaxiMart's **robot rollout** team in the first year.
**Automate** the jacket shop to a few hours and **squeeze** out every pound.
**Save** **£1,000** toward a city deposit by year end.
feel: **Alarmed**, which is unusual for someone who normally **calms** others.
S2.quote: In 2028 an AI can write listings and run an online shop better than I can, so my side business has no edge.
fieldNote: She sees her **side income** losing value as fast as her job.
She plans to ride the **three-year gap** by installing robots.
**Moving to the city** is new: the fast picture pushes her out of Kelby.

steps.text: Apply to join MaxiMart's robot rollout team in the first year
Use AI to cut the jacket shop to a few hours a week
Save £1,000 toward a city deposit by the end of the year
Move to the city where the store setup jobs are

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people start now, so start now. I'd post a list of free courses. At work I'd set up a little lunch session showing people the AI tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm okay if I'm quick. Five years gets me trained in store systems before AGI in 2031, and I'd be working with the robots when they arrive around 2034. The risk is MaxiMart hiring outside experts instead of training us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the retail systems certificate the MaxiMart group runs online, two evenings a week. I'd keep the jacket shop as pocket money and stop trying to grow it. And I'd ask Paul to put me down for any new tech in the store.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but quite excited. Like the first day at a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said MaxiMart might hire outside experts. What would you do if that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Apply to the experts' firm, honestly. If an outside firm is installing robots in every store, they'll need people who know how shops actually run. I'd sell myself as the one who knows the customer side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still leave Kelby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not in this one. Five years means I could save and move when I've got a job lined up, not before. That's the sensible way.

S3.quote: If an outside firm is installing robots in every store, they'll need people who know how shops actually run.

steps.text: Take MaxiMart's online retail systems certificate two evenings a week
Run a lunch session showing colleagues the store's AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is loads of time, so this is a chance, not a threat. People should try one new thing a year. I'd post that as a challenge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd feel fairly good. I'll be thirty-seven when the robots reach the shop floor in 2039, and by then I want to be running a store team or a setup crew. The thinking side changes earlier, but I'm already in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd go for the trainee manager scheme and grow the jacket shop. In a couple of years I'd do the systems certificate. And I'd put fifty a month into a savings account I can't easily touch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. I like having time to do things properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Is there anything that could still go wrong for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting stuck in Kelby, honestly. If MaxiMart closes the store or sells it, there's nothing else here. That's the bit I can't plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the store closed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Move, straight away, with whatever I'd saved. The jacket shop goes wherever I go, so that's something. I'd rather start again in a city than wait in an empty car park.

say: Ten years makes this a **chance**, not a **threat**.
Shop workers should try **one new thing** every year, starting with the tools at work.
think: By **thirty-seven** she wants to run a store team or a setup crew.
Her real risk is getting **stuck in Kelby** if the store closes.
do: **Apply** for the **trainee manager** scheme this year.
**Do** the **systems certificate** in a couple of years.
**Put** **£50 a month** into a locked savings account.
feel: Mostly **calm**, glad of **time** to do things properly.
S4.quote: I'd rather start again in a city than wait in an empty car park.
fieldNote: The decade gives her **room** to climb inside MaxiMart first.
Her one fear is **local closure**, since there's no other employer.

steps.text: Apply for MaxiMart's trainee manager scheme this year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because both my job and my side business lose their edge at once and I've got no cushion to move. What would help is a paid way into the robot setup jobs for people already on the shop floor. And help with a deposit if you have to move for work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people who don't speak English. I translate for a family from my street every week, and a machine can translate words, but it doesn't notice when someone is scared.

headlineQuote: A machine can translate words, but it doesn't notice when someone is scared.
portrait: Daria, 27, is the **self-checkout host** at the MaxiMart hypermarket in Kelby.
She rents a room, has about **three weeks** saved, and sells **vintage jackets** online.
She uses **AI every day** and enjoys change, calling a quiet world almost disappointing.
She aims to join the teams that **install robots** in stores, using the three-year gap.
She is **uneasy** in slow worlds and **alarmed** at AGI by 2028, when her side business also loses its edge.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028**, when her job and **side business** lose their edge together.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid route** into robot setup jobs for shop-floor staff.
Help with a **deposit** if she has to move for work.
